passage: A parable that became famous in the second half of the twentieth century asks us to imagine a pasture open to all. Each herder, reasoning that the benefit of an extra animal is his alone while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, adds another, and then another, until the grass is gone and all are ruined. The moral usually drawn is stark: resources held in common will be destroyed unless they are divided into private plots or placed under the control of the state.

The parable is persuasive, but it describes something that most actual commons are not. In many villages, pastures, woodlots, fishing ponds and irrigation channels have been shared for generations without being exhausted, and not because the villagers were unusually selfless. They were governed by rules. A household might be allowed to graze only as many animals as it could feed through the winter from its own fields; grazing might move between sections of the hill in a fixed rotation; a watchman, paid in grain, might patrol the boundary, and offenders might face fines that rose with each repeated offence. The herders of the parable have no such rules, no means of watching one another and no way of punishing those who cheat. What the parable describes is not a commons but open access, a resource that belongs to no community at all.

This does not mean that village commons always survive. They tend to fail in recognisable circumstances: when outsiders who are not bound by local rules can enter freely, when a distant authority overrides local arrangements with regulations that villagers neither understand nor respect, when migration thins the community so much that no one is left to keep watch, or when a sudden rise in the value of the resource makes cheating more tempting than it has ever been. These are real dangers. But they are dangers to particular institutions, not proof that shared ownership is doomed by human nature.

The practical lesson is that the familiar choice between private property and state control is too narrow. To say so is not to romanticise village life; such arrangements can be strict, and some are unequal, giving larger shares to households that hold more land. Even so, a third possibility, communities managing their own resources by rules they have made and can enforce, has a long record of success, and policy that ignores it may destroy working arrangements in the name of preventing a tragedy that was never going to happen.

passage: A familiar picture of the responsible thinker holds that she believes nothing on another's say-so until she has satisfied herself that the speaker is reliable. On this view, testimony is a second-class source of knowledge, legitimate only when it can be cashed out in the currency of one's own perception and reasoning: I may believe the timetable because I have found timetables accurate before, and I may believe my doctor because I have, or could obtain, evidence of her competence. The picture has the appeal of self-reliance. It seems to keep the knower in charge of what she knows.

The difficulty is that almost nobody could meet its demands, and the few who tried would know very little. Consider how much of what an ordinary adult believes was simply told to her: the shape of the continents, the date of her own birth, the existence of cells, the fact that a city she has never visited lies where the maps place it. To check the reliability of these sources she would have to rely on further sources, whose reliability would in turn need checking. The independent track record the picture asks for is itself largely assembled from testimony. A child who refused to believe her teachers until she had verified their credentials would never acquire the language in which credentials are described.

It does not follow that we may believe whatever we are told. The better view is that a hearer is entitled to accept what she is told unless she has some reason for doubt: a speaker with an evident motive to deceive, a claim that collides with what she already has good grounds to believe, a manner that suggests guesswork rather than knowledge. On this view the burden is reversed. Trust is the default, and it is suspicion, not acceptance, that must be earned by evidence. This is not credulity, because the default is sensitive to defeaters; the hearer who ignores a glaring sign of deceit is not exercising her entitlement but neglecting it.

Defenders of the stricter picture are right about one thing. A default of trust is only as good as the hearer's alertness to the signals that should override it, and that alertness is unevenly distributed and easily exploited. The con artist's whole craft consists in suppressing the cues that would trigger doubt. But this shows that we need to cultivate sensitivity to defeaters, not that we must abandon trust as a starting point. A community in which everyone demanded proof before belief would not be more rational than ours; it would merely be poorer in what it could collectively know.

passage: It has become common for conservation projects and agricultural agencies to announce that they have 'validated' some piece of local knowledge. Fishers' accounts of where a species gathers to spawn are checked against tagging data; herders' claims about which plants their animals avoid in a dry year are tested in feeding trials; farmers' weather signs are compared with rainfall records. When the local claim survives, it is welcomed into the scientific literature, and the project is praised for taking seriously people whose expertise was long ignored. This is an improvement on simple dismissal. Yet the language of validation carries assumptions that deserve more scrutiny than they usually receive.

The first is that local knowledge is a set of separate statements, each of which can be lifted out and checked on its own. Much of what farmers and fishers know does not take this form. A farmer who decides when to sow may attend at once to the flowering of a particular tree, the behaviour of ants, the smell of the soil and the memory of the last three seasons, weighing them against one another in ways she could not easily put into words. Test any one of these signs in isolation and it may predict rainfall poorly; to conclude that the farmer's knowledge has failed would be to mistake a judgement for a list of rules. What is being evaluated is not what she knows but a fragment translated into a form the evaluator can handle.

The second assumption is that the direction of authority runs one way. Science sets the standard, local knowledge applies for admission, and once admitted it belongs to the literature rather than to the people who held it. Communities have sometimes found that knowledge about medicinal plants or fishing grounds, once published, was used by outsiders in ways they had no say in. Validation, in other words, can be a means of transfer as much as of recognition.

It would be wrong to conclude that local knowledge should be shielded from testing altogether. Some local beliefs are mistaken, as some scientific ones are, and the communities that hold them revise them in the light of experience more often than romantic accounts allow. The objection is not to checking but to a procedure in which only one side checks. Where farmers help decide which questions are asked and how the results will be used, and where scientific claims are also tested against their observations, the two bodies of knowledge can correct each other. That is a more demanding arrangement than validation, and a more honest one.

passage: Arguments about working from home usually turn on a single question: are people as productive at the kitchen table as they are at the office desk? For many experienced professionals the honest answer appears to be yes, or close enough. They know their jobs, they know whom to ask, and they gain hours that once disappeared into commuting. But the question is framed around the output of a worker who is already competent, and it says little about how anyone becomes competent in the first place.

Consider a hypothetical accounting firm that sends everyone home. Its partners notice no fall in billable work during the first year, and the move looks like a clear success. What they cannot see is what their newest recruits are missing. In an office, a junior accountant overhears a senior colleague talking a nervous client through a bad result, watches how a disputed figure is checked, and asks a quick question that would feel too trivial to put in an email. None of this appears in any measure of output, and almost none of it is deliberately taught. It is absorbed, in the way apprentices have always absorbed a trade, by being near people who practise it.

Remote arrangements tend to remove exactly this kind of learning, because it depends on unplanned exposure and remote work is organised around planned contact. A video call is scheduled, has an agenda and ends when the agenda is done. The junior who would have learnt by watching instead learns only what someone remembered to explain. The cost is real but delayed: it shows up years later, as a cohort of mid-career staff who are slower to exercise judgement than their predecessors were at the same stage, by which time the decision that caused it has long been forgotten.

This is not an argument for ordering everyone back to their desks. Offices have never guaranteed this kind of learning; a junior placed among seniors who keep their doors shut learns little more than one at home. Firms can also try to replace accidental exposure with deliberate arrangements, such as pairing juniors with seniors on live work or inviting them to sit in on difficult calls. The point is that such arrangements must be built on purpose, and a firm that judges remote work only by the output of its experienced staff will not notice that it needs them until the damage is done.

passage: When a language is said to be endangered, the response that attracts the most attention is documentation. Linguists record the last fluent speakers telling stories, explaining how to build a house or prepare a medicine, conjugating verbs on request; the recordings are transcribed, annotated and deposited in archives designed to outlast the people who made them. Such projects are routinely described as saving the language, and the phrase is meant sincerely. Something irreplaceable is, after all, being kept from disappearing.

But what is kept is not quite a language. A language, in the sense that matters to its speakers, is a practice: it is what people do when they greet one another, quarrel, court and console, and its existence consists in the fact that children acquire it from those around them. An archive holds evidence of that practice, often superb evidence, but it no longer holds the practice itself. To say that a recorded language has been saved is a little like saying that a photographed forest has been conserved. The photographs may be invaluable to someone who later tries to replant; they are not the trees.

The distinction would be pedantic if it did not affect what gets done. It does. Documentation produces outputs that funders and universities know how to count: hours of recording, entries in a dictionary, a published grammar. Supporting transmission produces almost nothing of the kind. It means paying for a language nest in which grandparents look after toddlers, defending a family's decision to speak the home language against the advice of a doctor or a teacher, or making it possible for young adults to earn a living without moving to a city where the language is of no use to them. These efforts are slow, uncertain and hard to evaluate, and when resources are short, the countable work tends to win.

None of this is an argument against archives. Where a community later sets out to bring back a language that has ceased to be spoken at home, the quality of the earlier documentation can decide how much of it can be recovered, and descendants have had reason to be grateful for the patience of a recorder who wrote down what their grandparents' generation did not pass on. The mistake is to treat documentation as the rescue rather than as insurance against the rescue failing. Where speakers still exist and children could still learn from them, the record is the second-best outcome, and a policy that spends most of its effort on it has quietly accepted defeat.

passage: For much of the last century, the standard official response to an informal settlement was to remove it. Planners looked at a hillside of self-built houses, narrow lanes and improvised water connections and saw a problem of housing quality, to be solved by demolition and the construction of orderly blocks elsewhere, usually on cheaper land at the edge of the city. The logic seemed humane as well as tidy: people living without drains or secure walls would be given drains and secure walls. That the residents frequently resisted, and that many of the new blocks were half empty within a few years, was read as ingratitude, or as evidence that the poor did not know their own interests.

A different reading is now more common, and it is more persuasive. An informal settlement is not simply a stock of poor dwellings; it is a working arrangement of livelihoods, and its location is usually its chief asset. A family that sells cooked food near a bus depot, a tailor who takes in work from a nearby market, a mother whose children attend a school within walking distance: all of them chose the site because of what it is close to. Relocation to a distant estate improves the walls while destroying the arrangement. The household may gain a toilet and lose two hours a day to travel, or lose the income that made the new rent payable at all. Seen this way, the empty blocks were not a puzzle but a verdict.

Upgrading in place starts from this recognition. Instead of replacing the settlement, it adds what is missing: paved lanes, drainage, water and sewer lines, street lighting and, crucially, some form of secure tenure, so that residents can invest in their houses without fearing that the next official survey will mark them for demolition. Because the residents remain where they are, the networks that sustain them survive, and the public money spent goes into infrastructure rather than into reproducing, at great cost and in the wrong place, a community that already existed.

None of this makes upgrading a universal remedy. Some settlements stand on land that floods every monsoon or slides in heavy rain, and to improve them in place is to invest in a future disaster. Nor is upgrading automatically benign: lanes widened for drainage can require the demolition of some houses, and a programme that installs pipes but withholds tenure leaves residents improved and still insecure. The case for upgrading is therefore not that informal settlements are good as they are, a romantic view their residents rarely share. It is that the people who built them understood something about the city that the planners who wished to clear them did not.

passage: Few questions in criticism have been argued so long, or with so little sign of settlement, as whether the meaning of a work is what its author intended. The intentionalist says yes: a text is an utterance, utterances are made by someone for a purpose, and to ignore that purpose is to read not the work but a sequence of marks that happens to resemble it. The anti-intentionalist says no: the author's state of mind is usually unavailable, frequently confused and in any case beside the point, since a published work belongs to the public language in which it was written, and its meaning is whatever that language, competently read, makes of it.

Each side wins its arguments by making the other's view look absurd, and each is right about what it denies. The intentionalist is right that we cannot read without attributing purposes. To notice that a sentence is ironic, that a repetition is deliberate or that a sudden plainness of style marks a turning point is already to treat the text as the product of choices; strip away every assumption about purpose and the irony vanishes along with the design. The anti-intentionalist is right that a letter to a newspaper or a diary entry in which the author explains what the book means has no special authority over the book. Authors misremember, revise their motives after the fact and sometimes simply misjudge what they have made.

The mistake common to both is to picture intention as a private event lying behind the text, which the text either reports faithfully or conceals. Intention in writing is better understood the way we understand it in action. We do not usually discover what someone meant by watching them and then consulting their inner life; we read the purpose in the shape of what they did. In the same way the intentions that matter to criticism are those embodied in a work's choices, its emphases and omissions, the expectations it sets up and then disappoints. They are public because the work is.

This view does not make the author irrelevant, nor does it make the author final. A writer's notebooks may help us see a pattern we had missed, as the testimony of a witness may help a court, but the evidence is then the pattern, not the testimony. And a work may carry implications its author never foresaw and would perhaps have disowned: a novel written to celebrate a way of life can, through the very details it lovingly records, reveal the costs that way of life imposed on those at its margins. To point this out is not to defy the author's intention but to take the work's design more seriously than its author's later account of it.

passage: Neutrality has a poor reputation among people who think seriously about war. To its critics it looks like a refusal to choose, a way for a small state to sit out the great moral contests of its time while others pay the price of deciding them. On this view the neutral is a free rider at best and a quiet collaborator at worst, trading with whichever side is winning and calling its caution a principle. The charge is not baseless, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what neutrality has usually been for the states that practised it with any success.

For a small country surrounded by larger ones, neutrality is less a moral posture than a strategy, and a demanding one. Its purpose is to remove the country from the calculations of its neighbours, to persuade each of them that the territory will never be used as a road or a base by the others. That persuasion does not come from declarations. It has to be earned through a long record of evenhanded conduct, through refusing favours that would look like alignment, and, above all, through an army strong enough to make occupation expensive. The neutral that cannot defend its borders is not neutral in any meaningful sense; it is simply unclaimed, and unclaimed ground in wartime is soon claimed.

Seen this way, neutrality is not passivity but a continuous effort of a particular kind. The neutral state must be ready to resist whichever side violates its frontier first, which means it must arm against all of its neighbours at once rather than against one. It must also be disciplined in peacetime, since a single treaty of friendship, a preferential trade deal or a careless remark by a minister can be read abroad as a signal of where it would stand in a crisis. Few alliances ask as much of their members as this solitary commitment asks of a country that has chosen it.

None of this guarantees success. Neutrality works only so long as the great powers judge that respecting it costs them less than violating it, and when a neutral's territory becomes essential to someone's war plans, even a well-armed and scrupulous record may count for little. Nor does the strategic defence settle every moral question; a neutral that profits handsomely from a war it claims to stand apart from invites the suspicion its critics voice. But the critics usually ask the wrong question. They ask whether neutrality is admirable, when the more useful question is whether, for a particular state in a particular place, it is the course most likely to keep that state's people out of a war they could not win.

passage: Critics of political language have long treated the slogan as its lowest form. A slogan, they point out, asserts nothing that could be checked. Words such as renewal, fairness, security or change are compatible with almost any programme, and a campaign that rallies behind one of them has, in effect, declined to say what it will do. On this account the vagueness of the slogan is a species of evasion, and the remedy is to demand specifics: costed proposals, timetables, named measures that a voter can hold against the candidate once the votes have been counted.

There is a good deal of sense in this, but it rests on a picture of the voter as an individual buyer comparing the contents of rival packages. Politics in most large societies does not work like that. A party seeking a majority must assemble people whose interests and hopes overlap only partly: the worker and the small employer, the city and the countryside, the young and the retired. A precise programme would divide them at once, since each specific measure pleases some members of the coalition at the expense of others. A slogan holds them together by offering a phrase into which each can read a version of what he or she wants. Its emptiness is not a failure of communication; it is what allows a heterogeneous coalition to communicate with itself at all.

To see the slogan in this way is not to absolve it, for the difficulty has merely been postponed. A coalition assembled on an open phrase must, once it wins, translate the phrase into decisions, and each decision closes off some of the readings that brought supporters in. Those whose reading is closed off do not usually feel that a compromise has been struck; they feel that a promise has been broken, and in a sense they are right, since the slogan let each of them believe that it had been made to them. The disillusionment that so regularly follows electoral victory is often attributed to the cynicism of politicians, but a good deal of it is built into the structure of the appeal. Vagueness borrows support from the future, and the future presents the bill.

Nor is the critics' remedy as clean as it looks. A detailed platform has its own dishonesty, of a quieter kind. It implies a control over events that no government possesses, and its specific commitments are routinely overtaken by a recession, a war or some crisis that no one foresaw. A voter who holds a government to the letter of such a platform may end up rewarding rigidity over judgement. Specificity, in other words, can be as much a performance as vagueness is, a display of seriousness staged for an audience that has learned to distrust slogans.

What, then, should a careful listener ask of political language? Not that it abandon general phrases, which coalitions cannot do without, nor that it supply a detailed plan for every contingency. A more useful question is whether the speaker, pressed on how the slogan would decide a real conflict between its own supporters, can name the principle that would settle it. A slogan backed by such a principle is simply a commitment stated at a high level of generality, and it can be held to account at that level. One that dissolves into a different answer for each audience that asks is merely a mirror, and it is the mirror, not the generality, that deserves the critics' contempt.

passage: Arguments about the cleaning of old paintings tend to repeat themselves with remarkable fidelity. A famous canvas is cleaned; the removal of darkened varnish reveals colours far brighter than anyone living has seen on it; and two parties form at once. One celebrates the recovery of what the painter actually intended, a picture freed from centuries of grime. The other mourns the loss of a mellow harmony that generations had loved, and suspects that the cleaners, in their zeal, have removed not only dirt but the delicate final glazes with which the painter softened his effects.

It is tempting to treat this as a contest between truth and sentiment, with the cleaners on the side of truth. There is something to this. Natural resin varnishes do yellow and darken with age, and a sky that now looks olive may well have been painted as a clear blue; to prefer the olive because one is used to it is to prefer an accident over a decision. Cleaning has repeatedly shown that painters long thought murky were in fact bold colourists, and no honest account of the debate can pretend otherwise.

Yet the cleaners' strongest claim, that they return the painting to its original state, is harder to sustain than it sounds. Pigments themselves change: some blues fade, some greens turn brown, some reds lose their glazes to light long before any restorer arrives. Removing the varnish from such a picture does not take it back to the day it left the studio; it produces a new object, one in which unchanged passages and altered ones sit side by side in proportions the painter never saw. The bright painting revealed by cleaning may therefore be no closer to the original than the dark one it replaced, only differently distant from it.

What follows is not that cleaning should stop, but that it should be described honestly. Every restoration is a judgement about which of a painting's many histories to favour, and judgements can be wrong. The responsible course is to make such judgements in ways that can be undone where possible, to record exactly what has been removed and why, and to abandon the language of revelation in favour of the language of interpretation. A restorer who says 'this is what the painter meant' claims more than any evidence can give; one who says 'this is our best reading, and here is how we reached it' claims only what the craft can support.

passage: Every few years a new survey announces that trust in public institutions has fallen again. Respondents are asked how much confidence they have in parliament, the courts, the police or the press, their answers are averaged, and the declining line is offered as evidence of a crisis. The finding is treated as self-interpreting: less trust is bad, more trust is good, and the task of leaders is to restore it. Each step of that reasoning deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives.

Begin with what the question measures. A person asked how far she trusts the courts may be reporting her estimate of their competence, her view of their honesty, her approval of recent verdicts, or simply her mood about public life in general. Answers about quite different institutions tend to rise and fall together, which suggests that much of what is captured is a general disposition rather than a considered judgement about any particular body. Nor does the answer reliably predict conduct. People who tell interviewers that they distrust the courts continue to sign contracts that only courts can enforce, and people who profess little confidence in the health service continue to take the medicines it prescribes. If trust is fundamentally a matter of what we are prepared to rely on, the survey and the behaviour can come apart, and it is not obvious that the survey is the better witness.

A second difficulty is that falling trust is ambiguous even where it is real. It may mean that institutions have become less reliable. It may also mean that citizens have come to expect more of them, or that information about their failures, once hidden, now circulates freely. In the last case the decline records not a deterioration in the institution but an improvement in the public's knowledge of it. The philosophical point beneath this is simple and often forgotten: trust is valuable only when it is placed in what is trustworthy. A population that trusted a corrupt police force completely would not be enjoying a civic good; it would be making a mistake, and one that the corrupt would be glad to exploit. What we should want is not high trust but well-calibrated trust, trust that rises and falls with the reliability of its object.

This does not license complacency. Distrust, warranted or not, has consequences of its own. Citizens who doubt that taxes are spent honestly may be readier to evade them; communities that expect the police to be indifferent may stop reporting crimes, which in turn makes the police less effective and the distrust more justified. A decline in measured trust can therefore be the beginning of a spiral that no recalibration will halt by itself, because the institution's reliability depends partly on the cooperation that distrust withdraws. The point is not that the numbers are meaningless but that they cannot, on their own, tell us whether we face a failing institution, a better-informed public or a passing mood.

What would tell us more is evidence of a different kind: whether expressions of trust track independent measures of institutional performance over time, whether people who say they distrust an institution still rely on it when something important is at stake, and whether trust differs between those who have dealt with an institution directly and those who know it only by reputation. Such evidence is harder to gather than a single question repeated every few years, and it yields no simple line on a chart for commentators to lament. That is precisely its value.

passage: Debates about intuition tend to fall into two camps that talk past each other. One camp collects cases in which experienced professionals, asked to explain a snap judgement, cannot say how they knew, and yet were right: the nurse who senses that a patient is deteriorating before the monitors register anything, the engineer who distrusts a design at a glance. The other camp collects cases in which confident experts did no better than simple formulas, or than chance, at predicting outcomes in their own fields. Each camp treats its own cases as the typical ones and the other camp's as curiosities.

A way through the impasse begins by asking what intuition is. On the most plausible account it is recognition: the rapid matching of a present situation to patterns stored from earlier ones, which brings with it a sense of what is likely to happen next and of what to do. Recognition of this kind can be only as good as the patterns it has learned, and patterns can be learned only where two conditions hold. The environment must contain regularities that link cues to outcomes, and the person must have had extensive practice with feedback quick and clear enough to reveal whether a judgement was right. A ward where patients either recover or worsen within hours satisfies both conditions. A market in which prices reflect the guesses of many other participants, and in which the consequences of a choice emerge slowly and mixed with luck, satisfies neither very well.

This account explains why both camps can find their cases. It also yields a less comfortable conclusion. The feeling of knowing that accompanies intuition is produced in the same way whether or not the underlying patterns are valid. A forecaster who has spent years in an environment with little regularity can feel as sure as a nurse, because confidence grows with familiarity and with the coherence of the story one can tell, not with accuracy. Subjective certainty therefore tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement. What tells us something is the environment in which the judgement was learned.

The practical upshot is not that intuition should be confined to a list of approved professions. The same expert may work in a high-validity environment for some tasks and a low-validity one for others. A clinician may become very good at judging, within minutes, whether a patient needs urgent attention, while long-range predictions about the same patient's recovery, whose outcomes arrive years later and are shaped by many intervening events, remain little better than guesses. The question to ask of any intuition, then, is not who holds it or how firmly, but whether the conditions for learning it were ever present.

passage: A recurring complaint about modern money holds that it lost its integrity when it ceased to be tied to gold. On this view, a currency backed by metal disciplines governments: they cannot issue what they do not hold, and so savers are protected from the slow erosion of their wealth by inflation. The appeal is easy to understand, since gold is tangible, scarce and ancient, while paper notes and electronic balances seem by comparison to be mere promises, and promises can be broken.

Yet the discipline the gold standard imposed was less a protection than a transfer of risk. Under a metallic standard, the quantity of money depended on the pace of mining and on the flow of metal between countries, neither of which had much to do with the needs of trade. When output grew faster than the stock of gold, prices had to fall, and falling prices are hard on anyone who owes money. A farmer who borrowed against next year's harvest found that the harvest fetched less while the sum he owed stayed exactly the same. Long stretches of gold discipline were therefore stretches in which debtors, who were usually the less wealthy, bore much of the cost of keeping money sound for their creditors.

Nor did the standard remove discretion from governments as completely as its admirers suggest. Countries suspended convertibility during wars and crises, altered the official price of gold, and managed their reserves with a good deal of judgement. The rule held while it was convenient and was set aside when it was not; what it chiefly removed was the ability to respond to a slump without first abandoning the rule itself, and many economic historians have observed that, in the depression of the 1930s, the countries that left gold earlier tended to recover earlier.

None of this means that the nostalgia is groundless. Its real object is not the metal but trust: people want assurance that whoever controls money will not debase it for short-term ends. That is a legitimate demand, and governments have given it plenty of justification, but it is better met by institutions whose conduct can be observed, questioned and corrected than by tying the supply of money to the accidents of geology. Gold offers the comfort of a rule that no one made; the difficulty is that a rule no one made is also a rule that no one can sensibly adjust when circumstances change.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, weather forecasting was imagined as a problem of insufficient detail. If the atmosphere obeyed known physical laws, then better observations and faster calculation should, in principle, allow the future to be computed as far ahead as anyone liked. The recognition that the atmosphere is chaotic, in the technical sense that tiny differences in its starting state grow until they dominate the outcome, seemed at first to end that hope. Beyond a horizon of a week or two, no conceivable improvement in measurement would make a single calculated forecast reliable, because no measurement can be perfect and every imperfection is eventually amplified.

What is striking is how the discipline turned this limit into a method. Instead of running a model once from the best available estimate of the present, forecasting centres now run it dozens of times, each from a starting state nudged slightly within the range of what observations allow. If the runs stay close together, the atmosphere is in a predictable mood and the forecast can be stated with confidence; if they fan out, the spread itself is the information, telling forecasters that several quite different outcomes remain live. Chaos, which looked like a verdict against prediction, became a way of measuring how much prediction a given situation permits.

Much of this gain is lost in the last step, when forecasts reach the public. A phone application that shows a single icon for Thursday, a cloud with three raindrops, has quietly discarded the ensemble and kept only something like its average. Users then judge the forecast by whether it rained, and a forecast that correctly said the outcome was uncertain is remembered as a forecast that was wrong. The habit is understandable, since most people want a decision rather than a distribution, but it trains the public to expect a kind of certainty the science has explicitly given up.

It would be a mistake, however, to treat the ensemble as a perfectly honest witness. Every run in it uses the same model, with the same simplified treatment of clouds, mountains and ocean surfaces, so errors built into the model are shared by all the members and do not show up as spread. An ensemble can therefore agree with itself and still be wrong, and forecasters spend considerable effort checking whether its spread matches the errors actually observed over many past forecasts. The spread is a measure of uncertainty, not a guarantee of it, and its value depends on that continual comparison with what the weather in fact did.

passage: It is often said that a book can be read for the first time only once, and the remark is usually meant as a lament. On a first reading we do not know what will happen; we are carried by suspense, surprised by turns we did not foresee, and moved in a way that, the argument goes, can never quite be recovered. Rereading, on this view, is a kind of nostalgia: a return to a place whose excitement has been used up, pleasant perhaps, but a lesser thing than the original encounter. Schools encourage the same view without meaning to, since a syllabus moves on once a book has been 'done', as though a single passage through it were the whole of the work. The lament has real feeling behind it, and anyone who remembers staying up late to finish a novel knows what it describes.

There is a case for the opposite view, that in an important sense only rereading is reading. A first reading is dominated by one question, what happens next, and that question consumes most of our attention. We skim descriptions to reach events, miss the significance of details whose importance has not yet been revealed and form judgements of characters that the book later overturns. Only when we know the ending can we attend to how the book reaches it: the early scene that quietly prepares a later one, the image that returns with altered meaning, the minor character whose remark, seemingly idle at first, turns out to state the novel's theme. Knowing the outcome does not empty these details; it fills them. Consider a novel built around a concealed secret. Read a second time, its hints, which at first seemed part of the scenery, stand out as hints, and the reader can admire the skill with which they were hidden in plain sight, a pleasure that the first reader, hurrying towards the revelation, could not have had.

Rereading also reveals a change in the reader. The novel read at fifteen and again at forty has not altered a word, yet it is a different book, because the person reading it has acquired experiences that let different passages speak. A story of a marriage that seemed, to the young reader, a tale of dull people becomes, to the older one, almost unbearably exact. Nothing on the page has moved; what has moved is the range of experience the reader can bring to it, and with it the passages that seem to matter. In this sense a book reread is a kind of instrument for measuring oneself, and the measurements are often humbling: we discover what we were once unable to see, and sometimes that the passages we admired most were the weakest.

None of this means that the first reading is worthless. It has a quality nothing later can supply, an innocence about what is coming that the writer counted on, and some effects are designed for it alone: the twist that recasts everything before it can surprise only once. Moreover, without a first reading there is nothing to reread, and the second encounter depends on the first even when it corrects it. Some books, indeed, are exhausted by one passage through them, and this is perhaps the most useful test of all. A book that offers nothing on a second reading was a mechanism for producing suspense, admirable in its way, while a book that gives more each time was something else. The difference between the two kinds is not visible from inside a first reading, which is one more reason to distrust the verdicts we reach there.

passage: Few political terms are used as loosely as populism. It is applied to movements of the left and of the right, to leaders who promise to spend lavishly and to those who promise to cut, to campaigns against banks and to campaigns against immigrants. A word that covers so much risks covering nothing, and some scholars have concluded that it is merely a label for whatever kind of politics the speaker happens to dislike. That conclusion is premature. The variety of populist programmes is real, but it may simply show that populism is not a programme at all.

Consider the most common attempt at definition: populism as hostility to elites. This cannot be sufficient, since criticism of the powerful is the ordinary business of opposition in any democracy, and a definition that made every challenger a populist would be useless. What distinguishes the populist is a further claim, namely that there exists a single, authentic people whose will is already known, and that the movement or leader in question alone gives it voice. Opponents are therefore not merely mistaken; they are illegitimate, and citizens who vote for them are not quite part of the people. On this account the core of populism is not anti-elitism but anti-pluralism, a refusal to accept that the people may be divided in good faith.

The value of this definition is that it explains a pattern which approaches based on policy tend to miss. A movement that claims to embody the whole people has difficulty accepting defeat, since a loss at the polls must then be explained as fraud, manipulation or the work of enemies; and once in office it is tempted to treat independent courts, a critical press or a neutral civil service as obstacles placed between the people and its rightful expression. None of this follows from hostility to elites alone. It follows from the claim to a moral monopoly of representation.

Yet the definition carries a hazard of its own. Precisely because it locates the danger in a style of claim rather than in a set of grievances, it can tempt those who use it to dismiss the grievances along with the style. Many people drawn to populist movements have real complaints: about decisions taken far away from them, about parties that seem interchangeable, about institutions that consult them rarely. To treat such voters as a symptom to be managed, rather than as citizens with reasons, is to deny them the standing that pluralism promises, and to confirm the populist story that an elite has stopped listening. The definition is a tool for recognising a threat to democratic competition; it is not a licence to stop asking why the threat finds an audience.

passage: Many of the long novels of the nineteenth century first reached their readers not as books but in instalments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more, in magazines or in separate parts. Modern criticism has tended to treat this fact as an extenuating circumstance. When such a novel sprawls, introduces a character it later forgets, or closes a chapter on a contrived moment of suspense, the serial is invoked as an excuse: the author was writing to deadline, paid by length, obliged to bring readers back next month. The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have, and that serial publication is a kind of noise to be filtered out.

The trouble with this view is that it treats the serial only as a set of pressures, when it was also a set of possibilities, and many of the qualities we now admire in these books grew from it. A novel read over eighteen months is lived with in a way that a novel read over a week is not. Its characters age alongside their readers; its crises arrive amid the readers' own. The large casts and interwoven plots that later critics found unwieldy were in part a response to this rhythm, since a reader returning after a month's absence needed several lines of interest to pick up, and recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place. What looks in a single volume like digression could, at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to.

Serial publication also made the novel unusually public while it was still unfinished. An instalment could be discussed before the next was written, and authors could, and sometimes did, adjust their plans in light of how readers responded. A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation, in which a book took shape partly through its encounter with an audience rather than being delivered complete to readers whose only role was to receive it. For a time the novel became a shared event, followed by readers who knew that a great many others were reading the same pages in the same weeks.

None of this is to deny the costs. Writing to fixed lengths did produce padding, and the demand for suspense at the end of each part did produce cliffhangers that the story did not need and that read awkwardly once the parts were bound together. A reader of the collected volume is entitled to notice these. What deserves suspicion is the standard against which they are judged as failures: the ideal of the novel as a single, unified design, conceived whole and executed according to plan. That ideal has a history of its own, and it gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions. Applied backward, it does not so much reveal the faults of serial fiction as convert its differences into faults.

There is, finally, an irony in the critical embarrassment. Long television dramas, released in episodes and discussed between them, are now often praised by critics for the very qualities, the slow accumulation, the large cast, the sense of a world lived alongside, that the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for. Nothing about the newer form proves the older one right, and a slack episode is no better for belonging to a celebrated series. But the shift in judgement suggests that what critics of the instalment novel took for timeless standards of form were, at least in part, the habits of one particular way of reading.

passage: Empathy enjoys a reputation that few other psychological capacities can match. To be told that one lacks it is an accusation; to call for more of it is to sound wise. Yet if empathy is understood in its strict sense, as the capacity to feel what another person feels, to be distressed by their distress and buoyed by their relief, there are reasons to doubt that it is a dependable guide to how we ought to act, however much it enriches how we live.

The trouble lies in its shape. Empathy works like a narrow beam: it illuminates whatever it is pointed at with great intensity and leaves everything else in darkness. It is most easily directed at people who are near us, who resemble us and who can be seen as individuals with faces and names. It is notoriously insensitive to number; the plight of one child described in detail can move us more than a report of thousands suffering in the same way, because thousands cannot be felt, only counted. A capacity with these properties will reliably favour the identifiable over the statistical, the familiar over the strange and the present over the future, and those are precisely the biases that moral reasoning is supposed to correct.

There is a darker possibility as well. Because empathy is felt for particular victims, it can be recruited against other people. An account of a single person wronged by a member of some group can stir a fierce sympathy that is then turned into demands for punishment of the whole group. The emotion in such cases is genuine; what is wrong is its range.

The obvious objection is that without empathy we would not care at all, and that a morality built only on principle would be bloodless. But this assumes that empathy is the only route to concern. Many people help strangers without imagining their way into the strangers' experience, out of a settled wish that others fare well, a sense of fairness, or the plain recognition that suffering is bad wherever it occurs. Psychologists sometimes distinguish empathy from compassion along these lines: the first means sharing another's feeling, the second means caring about another's good without necessarily sharing the feeling. Compassion, unlike empathic distress, does not exhaust the carer, and it can be extended to people one will never see.

None of this is an argument for coldness. In friendship, in parenting and in the consulting room, the ability to feel with another person is part of what makes the relationship what it is, and nobody would wish it away. The claim is narrower: that when we must decide how to allocate help across many people, or how to treat those we do not know, a feeling that shines only where it is pointed should be checked by judgement rather than trusted as the measure of what is right.

passage: Many people who would never tell a lie are perfectly comfortable misleading. Asked whether he has finished a report, an employee replies that he has been working on it all morning, which is true, and which he says precisely so that his manager will conclude that the report is nearly done. He has not lied, he tells himself; if his manager draws the wrong conclusion, that is her inference, not his assertion. The intuition behind this self-defence is widely shared, and it is not merely self-serving. Ordinary moral thinking, many legal systems and a long tradition of moral reasoning have treated the outright falsehood as a graver matter than the true statement artfully deployed.

Yet when we ask what is wrong with lying in the first place, the distinction begins to look thin. The harm of a lie consists chiefly in two things: the listener ends up with a false belief that he did not choose, and the trust he extended to the speaker has been turned against him. Both harms are present in the case of the employee. His manager now believes something false about the report, and she believes it because she assumed, reasonably, that a colleague answering her question was trying to answer it. The employee exploited exactly that assumption. That he did so by selecting true words rather than inventing false ones changes the technique, not the result.

There is, however, one setting in which the distinction earns its keep. In a negotiation over the price of a used car, both parties know that the other is pursuing its own advantage, and each is expected to read the other's statements with suspicion. A seller who says that several people have asked about the car, when several have indeed asked but none has made an offer, leaves the buyer free to discount the remark, and a competent buyer will. Where the listener is on guard by convention, the responsibility for drawing inferences is genuinely shared, and the misleader has exploited much less trust than the liar, who asserts something false that even a wary listener has no means of checking.

What this suggests is that the moral line runs less between lying and misleading than between relationships in which listeners are entitled to rely on a speaker's cooperation and those in which they are not. In the first kind, which includes most of our dealings with doctors, colleagues, friends and family, the careful choice of true but misleading words offers almost no moral shelter. In the second, it offers some. The employee who congratulates himself on never having lied has simply mistaken the setting he is in.

passage: Talk of moral progress makes many people uneasy. It sounds like the self-congratulation of every age that has looked back on its predecessors and found them wanting, and it seems to require a fixed standard against which the direction of change could be measured, a standard that is itself in dispute. Yet it is hard to describe the abolition of legal slavery, or the end of public torture as a form of entertainment, merely as changes in fashion, as though they were on a par with a shift in the length of coats. Most people who doubt the idea of moral progress in theory find themselves unable to give it up in particular cases.

One influential way of making sense of the idea is to describe progress as the expansion of a circle of concern. Early moral codes, on this telling, extended full consideration only to kin or to members of the tribe; over time the boundary has been pushed outward, to strangers, to foreigners, to people of other races and faiths, and, more recently and more contentiously, to animals. Progress consists in recognising as morally considerable those whom we previously ignored. The picture is appealing because it gives progress a direction without requiring agreement on a complete moral theory: one needs only the modest premise that arbitrary exclusion is a mistake. It also explains why reformers have so often described their work as opening the eyes of their contemporaries rather than changing their values: the values, on this telling, were already present, and only their application had been blocked.

The picture is not wrong, but it is incomplete in a way that matters. Some of the clearest cases of progress involve not who counts but what we owe to those who already counted. The view that a husband may beat his wife was not, in most societies that held it, a view that wives fell outside moral concern; wives were very much inside the circle, assigned a place in it that we now regard as degrading. Reform came not from widening the boundary but from revising the terms within it. The same is true of changing attitudes to children, who have always been objects of intense concern, and whose treatment has nonetheless been transformed.

There is also a danger in the circle image that its admirers tend to overlook. If progress is measured by the width of the circle, then any extension looks like an advance, and any contraction like a regression. But concern can be extended in ways that are themselves harmful: the circle of a missionary empire was wide, and that width was part of its justification for interfering in other people's lives. Inclusion that comes with a presumption of authority over the included is not obviously better than the indifference it replaces. What matters is not only that more beings are counted, but how they are counted.

None of this means that we should abandon the idea of moral progress. It means that progress is less like a single line along which societies advance and more like a series of corrections, each prompted by the discovery that some practice depended on a mistaken belief, an unexamined interest or a failure of imagination. Such corrections can be recognised as improvements without a finished theory of the good, in the way that a scientist can recognise an error without possessing the final truth. That is a more modest claim than the circle image offers, but it is also harder to dismiss as the vanity of the present.

options.C: Moral progress consists in extending moral concern to those beings who were previously left outside its boundary.
